items.content_html:

“Inside Gaza,” a 72-minute film following four Agence France-Presse (AFP) journalists reporting from Gaza, won the Best Documentary award and an audience award at Montreal’s Cinemania Film Festival on Nov. 14. The film follows the journalists during the first seven months after Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, documenting the risks and difficulties of reporting from a territory largely inaccessible to international media. Directed by Hélène Lam Trong, the documentary draws mainly on footage the journalists shot for AFP and interviews recorded after they left Gaza. AFP Gaza bureau chief Adel Zaanoun accepted the awards in Montreal and dedicated them to journalists killed in the war and those still working there. The film has won other festival awards and is eligible for consideration for the 2027 Oscars.

items.title: [elpais.com] Journalist's murder in Costa Rica raises alarm among regional press
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez Chaverri was shot dead on November 16, three days after an unknown person set fire to two cars and part of the home of Panamanian investigative journalist Rolando Rodríguez in Panama City. Following the killing in Santo Domingo de Heredia, Costa Rica, press organizations and the United Nations called for an investigation and warned of its chilling effect on journalism. Reporters Without Borders (RSF), an international organization that defends press freedom, said it had already raised the alarm about pressure on critical journalists and obstacles to reporting independently. A University of Costa Rica poll published on November 11 found that 58% of the population considers journalism dangerous to practice, and 54.7% believes freedom of expression is at risk. The Costa Rican Prosecutor's Office said it would examine Rodríguez's public allegations, the people he named, and other possible motives for the crime. It added that it seeks to identify both the perpetrators and those who ordered the killing. President Laura Fernández condemned the murder and said she had ordered the police forces to cooperate with the investigation.

London’s Metropolitan Police said on Friday, Nov. 13, that it had opened an investigation into allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving David Walliams, the British comedian and children’s author. Police said the new complaints were separate from allegations published by ITV News and The Guardian, but detectives are also reviewing those reports for evidence of offences. The reports accused Walliams of using his celebrity status to pursue young women and girls. One woman alleged he sexually assaulted her when she was 15, and others said he groomed them as teenagers. Walliams denies criminal wrongdoing and says he never abused his position. The Guardian and ITV said they spoke with more than 100 people during their three-year investigation. Police have not publicly detailed the number or circumstances of the new complaints. The force said specialist officers are supporting those who have come forward. Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney urged anyone affected to contact police, regardless of when an alleged offence took place.

items.title: [sci.news] Peruvian fossil reveals pygmy sperm whale with extreme skull asymmetry
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers have described Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale whose fossil skull shows the most extreme facial asymmetry documented in a cetacean, and possibly in any mammal. The animal lived in what is now southern Peru between 6.3 million and 5.6 million years ago and was about 2.7 meters long. Both bony nostrils sat on the left side of its skull. Its dense, downward-curving snout and flexible neck suggest it searched for food in shallow seabed sediments. Researchers propose that it used echolocation to locate buried prey; unlike some bottom-feeding marine mammals, it had no facial whiskers or other specialized sensory structures for foraging.

items.title: [eos.org] Arctic ice cores trace century-old toxic pollution to Montana mine
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers traced arsenic and other heavy metals preserved in 10 Arctic ice cores to the Anaconda Copper Mine in Montana, linking pollution to a single industrial source thousands of kilometers away. Arsenic levels in some cores reached about 15 times preindustrial levels around 1914, according to the study in Nature Sustainability. By combining ice-core measurements, atmospheric modeling and historical production records, the team estimated that about 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic levels associated with increased health risks between 1898 and 1918. Pollution-control equipment installed at the smelter in 1919 reduced emissions by roughly 60% to 65%, though the mine continued operating until 1947. Lead researcher Joseph McConnell, a climate and environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, said epidemiologists should investigate the pollution’s potential effects on people.

NASA said Swift detected about 20,000 ultraviolet sources there, many of them hot stars and star clusters obscured in visible-light views. Swift was designed to turn rapidly toward short-lived cosmic explosions and observe them in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light. It also alerted other observatories so they could follow events before they faded. The U.S. Space Force said Swift reentered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some pieces may have survived.

Communities across the United States are taking different approaches to police automated license-plate reader (ALPR) networks: voters in York, Maine, and League City, Texas, rejected their use, while Cedar Rapids approved a nearly $500,000 switch from Flock Safety to Axon without increasing its network of 70 cameras. Springfield, Massachusetts, has not advanced a proposed ban; councilors plan to review possible safeguards before deciding whether to send it forward. The systems record plates, timestamps and locations. Police say they can help investigate crimes and find missing people, while privacy advocates warn about tracking, misuse and data sharing beyond local jurisdictions. Suffolk County’s sheriff’s office has data-sharing relationships with slightly more than 400 agencies, established through system settings rather than formal written agreements. Ohio lawmakers are considering House Bill 725, which would set statewide rules for police use of plate data and make misuse a fifth-degree felony. The ACLU of Ohio argues the bill regulates data only after collection and could reduce public access to search information. Springfield’s committee plans to meet again after consulting the city’s Law Department.

Italy’s data-protection authority has set three deadlines for Meta to change Facebook’s Android gallery-suggestion feature, which drew an €805 million fine for accessing users’ photos without specific consent. Meta must report the work it has begun within 30 days, disable the feature by default and seek separate consent within 60 days, and report the measures taken within 90 days. Meta says it will appeal, calling the penalty disproportionate. The feature suggests photos and videos from a phone’s gallery for Facebook posts. The regulator found that the app used a single permission for several functions and a generic notice that did not clearly disclose gallery suggestions. About 20 million Android users in Italy were affected. The regulator based its decision on Italy’s implementation of the European Union’s ePrivacy rules, which it says require informed consent to access information stored on phones. The investigation did not assess whether Meta used gallery content to train artificial-intelligence models. Meta denies doing so. Italy’s authority said it could separately examine a 2026 feature that processes gallery content in the cloud.

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. items.title: [frontpageafricaonline.com] COP31 draft proposes $120 billion in annual adaptation finance by 2035
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A draft COP31 agreement proposes at least $120 billion a year in adaptation finance for developing countries by 2035, alongside accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels. Released by the conference presidency on Nov. 16, the text remains under negotiation and does not represent an agreed position; the talks in Antalya, Türkiye, are scheduled to end Nov. 20. African negotiators are pressing for predictable grants, measurable delivery milestones and finance that does not deepen debt. The United Nations Environment Programme estimates developing countries will need $305 billion annually for adaptation by 2035, while international public adaptation finance reached $28.2 billion to $31.7 billion in 2024. Ghanaian Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings also called for funding to restore land and rivers damaged by mining and for greater local processing of Africa’s minerals.

items.title: [abc.net.au] Lancet researchers urge health emergency declaration as climate losses mount
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The UK’s Climate Change Committee warned that loosening electric-vehicle sales rules could add 8.4 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions a year by the next decade and make the country likely to miss legally binding climate targets. The government is consulting on lowering the zero-emission vehicle requirement, which currently requires zero-emission vehicles to account for 80% of new car sales by 2030 and 100% by 2035. The committee says the rules account for the largest share of planned emissions cuts through 2037; weakening them would require comparable reductions elsewhere to meet the carbon budget for 2033-37. Its chair, Nigel Topping, also warned that reducing the targets would increase the UK’s exposure to volatile oil markets, while the government says the consultation will not change its stated phaseout dates for petrol and diesel vehicles.

items.content_html:

AI coding editor Cursor said an attacker used an access key exposed at its inference provider, Fireworks AI, to access internal data and place tampered Anthropic Claude Code extensions in Cursor’s marketplace on October 29. The two versions remained available for about 11 hours. As many as 5,000 users who requested them may have received the builds, but that figure does not confirm successful infections. The attacker found credentials in historical coding-agent traces from users who had not enabled Privacy Mode, then accessed selected Cursor services. Cursor said the attacker did not affect customer code repositories or official releases. It has cut off Fireworks access, rotated credentials and rebuilt the marketplace. It believes the incident is contained and advises affected developers to follow its cleanup guidance.

items.title: [ecdc.europa.eu] European disease agency warns resistant bacteria threaten hospital treatment
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) warned on Nov. 18 that antibiotic-resistant bacteria continue to spread across Europe, leaving doctors with fewer effective treatments. Its European Antibiotic Awareness Day alert called for urgent, sustained action. More than 35,000 people die each year from antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in the European Union and European Economic Area. More than 70% of Europe’s AMR health burden is linked to multidrug-resistant infections acquired in healthcare settings. The ECDC said resistant infections could make it harder or impossible to safely carry out organ transplants, cancer chemotherapy and intensive care. It called for coordinated infection prevention, careful antibiotic prescribing, stronger laboratory capacity and surveillance. Faster genomic monitoring can help track the spread of resistant strains and guide treatment decisions, it said.
